Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) ETFs recorded about $1 billion in weekly inflows in the week of April 17, according to SoSoValue. The figure marks the strongest week for Bitcoin ETF inflows since the $1.42 billion recorded in the week of January 16. The surge has increased optimism among BTC holders about whether ETF demand could drive more upside for BTC in Q2.

More importantly, Bitcoin ETFs have now posted 7 consecutive weeks of positive inflows. During that period, BTC climbed from $68,000 to above $80,000—a 17.6% upside over that period. We analyzed key factors driving Bitcoin ETFs right now and where BTC could be by the end of Q2 if this trend continues.

Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $5.30 billion in outflows between November 2025 and February 2026, which made a March recovery unlikely. But the funds reversed sharply, with massive inflows in March ($1.32 billion), April ($1.97 billion), and another $1.28 billion in the first 12 days of May alone.

In total, Bitcoin ETFs have now recorded $3.43 billion in combined inflows over the last seven weeks. BlackRock’s IBIT led the recovery, bringing in approximately $3 billion since April 2. The fund currently holds over 821,000 BTC—equal to roughly 3.91% of Bitcoin’s total supply—while ranking among the top 1% of all U.S. ETFs by inflow volume. Fidelity’s FBTC brought in the second-largest inflows during this period, with combined inflows of roughly $277.27 million.

Institutional investors across all levels are absorbing ETFs at a pace far above daily mining output, and that demand has been a primary driver of BTC’s Q2 recovery, tightening available supply and improving market sentiment to push Bitcoin above $80,000 for the first time since January 31.

Another key driver is the geopolitical instability that has capped the performance of crypto assets since February. While crypto assets struggled to break above key resistance levels and sellers dominated the market, investors viewed Bitcoin ETFs as a relatively safer alternative alongside assets like Gold and Oil. As global tensions intensified in March, many rotated capital into Bitcoin products, and this trend has continued into May.

If Bitcoin ETF inflows maintain their consistent monthly growth through the end of Q2, Bitcoin could break above $90,000 and potentially rally towards $100,000. Right now, institutional players are absorbing around 500% of Bitcoin’s daily mining output of 450 BTC. That 5:1 demand-to-supply ratio has sustained for weeks, helping BTC hold above $80,000.

Another factor keeping institutional players active is the expected passage of the CLARITY Act , which has added to ETF inflows momentum. On April 10, the American Bankers Association launched a last-minute lobbying campaign to pressure senators against the bill. But this didn’t stop Bitcoin ETFs from recording $27.29 million in inflows on April 11, as expectations that the bill would pass before the July 4 White House deadline offset the uncertainty that would have triggered outflows and bearish pressure.

In response, major policymakers and institutional players—like Coinbase’s Legal Officer Paul Grewal and Senator Bernie Moreno —have pushed back, with the Senate Banking Committee releasing a 309-page draft for the CLARITY Act today. A markup vote on May 14 would likely accelerate institutional inflows further, which could help Bitcoin reach and hold around $90,000—a 12.5% move from today’s level.

If Bitcoin maintains its reputation as a safer alternative in the market and ETF demand remains consistent, a Q2 close above $95,000 becomes a realistic base case. BTC can reach $150,000 if the CLARITY Act gets to Trump’s desk for signing before the end of June.
Bitcoin could reach $100,000 by the end of Q2 if two things hold: ETF inflows maintain their current pace and the market gets regulatory clarity with the CLARITY Act passage.

If the bill advances through the Senate in May and reaches President Donald Trump before the end of June, Bitcoin would rally on the back of regulatory clarity and ETF demand, with the combined momentum giving BTC the runway to push above $100,000.

But if the CLARITY Act is delayed into 2027, it could slow down institutional momentum—which could reintroduce uncertainty about crypto regulations in the U.S. Such a delay could weaken ETF demand and trigger outflows—which would see BTC lose the $80,000 support level.

The market is balancing a familiar seasonal tailwind against a near-term macro test.
For the rest of October, the conditions are more important than the calendar label.
Traders will be watching Treasury yields, inflation signals, interest-rate expectations, and geopolitical developments alongside Bitcoin's price action.
BTC USD trades near $86,400 on Friday, October 2, up about 3.1% over 24 hours, as Bitcoin extends its third straight weekly gain.
Traders are betting on October's strong track record, but the U.S. nonfarm payrolls report due later today could reset expectations for Federal Reserve rates.
Bitcoin has gained in 10 of the past 15 Octobers.
Positive months averaged gains of 27.4%, while negative ones averaged losses of 13%.
Bitcoin hit a record near $126,000 early that month, then closed October lower as risk appetite faded.
Employment releases can move Bitcoin through their effect on rate expectations, rather than through any direct link between payrolls and the Bitcoin network.
Macro pressure is not limited to the jobs report.
The reported risks also include persistent U.S.-Iran tensions and the prospect of rising interest rates, both of which could weigh on investor willingness to hold risk assets.
A favorable seasonal pattern does not insulate Bitcoin from those broader forces.
Bitcoin is up 2.6% this week after a 6.4% rise in September, its third monthly gain in a row.
Still, it sits about 1.5% below its yearly open near $87,700, after falling as low as $58,000 earlier in 2026.
On the chart, Bitcoin has now cleared the $85,000 resistance zone that capped it for nearly a week.
The next hurdle is $87,400, the September 21 high.
A rise above that area does not settle the larger question of whether Bitcoin can hold its recovery if macro conditions turn less supportive.
A rising Bitcoin price can lift sentiment across crypto, but individual tokens still respond to their own catalysts, and a positive market session does not mean every asset is participating equally.

sources.title: AI is fueling a new battle over health care costs
passages: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence in the health care system is creating another source of pressure on costs that are already climbing, adding to the squeeze on consumers who are also facing higher prices for fuel and groceries.
How AI will ultimately impact health care costs may depend on what financial incentives are built into the system.

It is also pushing up costs for employers to provide health coverage to their employees, with one industry survey anticipating costs could rise as much as 11% next year unless they cut benefits or pass those increases onto their workers.
Hospitals and insurance companies are increasingly using AI tools to maximize payments for care or control costs, ramping up tensions over the cost of care and who pays for it.

While the technology’s supporters say it could help improve treatment and make the system more efficient and eventually cheaper, its growing use in billing and coverage decisions may already be pushing costs higher. A recent report produced by the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, which represents state Blue Cross plans, claimed hospitals using AI tools has already contributed to nearly $1 billion in additional expenses over two years by claiming patients had more challenging illnesses to treat. According to the report, hospitals submitted claims for tens of thousands of patients describing their illnesses as more medically complex over the last two years compared to 2023. But even with added conditions, the insurers found no evidence patients had received additional or different treatments from hospitals. The report said that hospitals are using AI tools to collect more information about their patients and using it to submit more expensive claims without improving treatment. “If patients are truly sicker, we'd expect to see more treatment,” Luke Chalker, BCBSA’s senior vice president of product and data science, said in a release. “For example, we're seeing significantly more anemia diagnoses at these hospitals without a corresponding increase in transfusions. The disconnect between diagnoses and treatment suggests that AI is identifying more billable conditions, not sicker patients.” Hospitals have disputed the insurance industry’s framing of using AI for medical coding and rejected claims they are inflating bills. Companies and industry groups have argued the technology is helping providers more accurately capture their patients’ conditions and accused insurers of using automated tools to challenge claims and deny payments for care. “These claims not only ignore the numerous underlying drivers of changes in coding intensity, including an aging patient population, but also overlook the legal, ethical and contractual obligations on hospitals to ensure appropriate coding,” the American Hospital Association wrote in an August fact sheet. Hospitals and insurance companies have been in a lengthy game of finger-pointing for years as the costs of healthcare have continued to spike in the U.S. with medication, patient care and operations all growing more expensive. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said recently that AI’s impact is going to make healthcare more expensive before it gets cheaper. "Short term, AI is going to be inflationary because it's going to turbocharge the ability of the current billing systems to work more effectively," Oz said at a summit held by Oracle last week. How AI will ultimately impact health care costs may depend on what financial incentives are built into the system. There is some belief that integrating AI into the healthcare system will ultimately lead to lower prices by reducing the resources spent on administrative functions, which can then be passed onto patients through lower bills. But whether that comes to fruition may depend on how medical care is billed. “AI has the ability to make the cost curve go in either direction, depending on the payment model. The more we get America into value-based care models, the more AI will actually help make those models work better and help people save more money. Those in fee-for-service will use AI to create more access, more appointments, more tests, more procedures, and better revenue cycle management, which will make healthcare more expensive,” Bob Kocher, a former Biden administration healthcare official and partner at Venrock, said during a Johns Hopkins panel discussion last week. Uncertainties about AI’s impact on health care come as Americans and their employers are already facing rapidly rising expenses. The U.S. already spends more on healthcare than any other country, accounting for nearly one-fifth of its entire gross domestic product. Health care and insurance premiums have continued to climb well above the rate of inflation in recent years, adding to stresses on household budgets and forcing some Americans to decide whether they can afford to see the doctor. It is also pushing up costs for employers to provide health coverage to their employees, with one industry survey anticipating costs could rise as much as 11% next year unless they cut benefits or pass those increases onto their workers. Facing higher premiums, deductibles and co-pays means workers are forced to pay for a larger share of their medical bills, an issue that may be even further exacerbated by AI tools. The issue has been the subject of several congressional hearings as lawmakers question how automated tools are impacting care and being used to make decisions about medical claims and coverage.

sources.title: Slovenia’s .si domain sees a surge in registrations after Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ order
passages: The domain name was commonly associated with Slovenia, where, ironically, First Lady Melania Trump is from.

Klara Herman, a spokesperson at Registry SI, the official organization that manages Slovenia’s domains, told the BBC earlier this week that there was a 2,199% increase in .si domain name purchases in September.
However, she was cautious about linking the boost only to President Trump.

Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet.
“A few founder friends are buying too ’cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued.
“Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.”
We reached out to a few other web hosting sites to see if they had seen similar trends.
GoDaddy said they don’t yet host the .si domain, and Squarespace hadn’t yet responded as of the time of publication.
Wix, interestingly enough, said that they weren’t seeing any “meaningful uptick” on their end, and that it’s been minimal on the site since September 29.
“It’s still early so that could change,” a Wix spokesperson said.

Still, the Registry noted 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30, the day after President Trump signed the executive order , and almost 13,000 new .si domain names were registered in the past 24 hours.

“Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .ai and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury.
For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment.

extraction.body: In not-so-surprising news, the .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump signed an executive order mandating all government agencies to refer to “AI” and “artificial intelligence” as “SI” and “super intelligence.” It echoes what happened at the start of the AI boom, when interest in the .ai domain name — associated with the country Anguilla — spiked and brought in millions for the island territory. Now it’s .si’s turn in the spotlight. The domain name was commonly associated with Slovenia, where, ironically, First Lady Melania Trump is from. Klara Herman, a spokesperson at Registry SI, the official organization that manages Slovenia’s domains, told the BBC earlier this week that there was a 2,199% increase in .si domain name purchases in September. However, she was cautious about linking the boost only to President Trump. Still, the Registry noted 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30, the day after President Trump signed the executive order , and almost 13,000 new .si domain names were registered in the past 24 hours. We reached out to a few other web hosting sites to see if they had seen similar trends. GoDaddy said they don’t yet host the .si domain, and Squarespace hadn’t yet responded as of the time of publication. Wix, interestingly enough, said that they weren’t seeing any “meaningful uptick” on their end, and that it’s been minimal on the site since September 29. “It’s still early so that could change,” a Wix spokesperson said. But web hosting platform Hostinger told me that .si is now its second most popular domain extension, right after .com. It found that among its customers, almost 4,300 registered .si on September 30 and about 5,400 on October 1; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in the last two days. It found that more than half the buyers were coming from the U.S. and India. Curiously enough, on Hostinger, only around 3% of the .si domains are explicitly related to AI, it said. Most are “unclassified” — meaning their names don’t match any specific category. It said that most of those registering the .si domain name seem to be people and businesses, though there is a speculative element, in that people could be buying the domains to resell them later. Upon hearing this, my first thought went back to what a founder messaged me earlier this week, noting that .si domains were reselling for over a million dollars. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, who specializes in working with AI and crypto founders, told me that he already bought the .si version of his company name “to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai.” And did so because it was cheap, so he figured he might as well “secure it now than potentially pay a lot more later.” Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet. “A few founder friends are buying too ’cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued. “Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.” There is a chance that .si could become pretty popular. President Trump’s executive order said that “the capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence,” and that they “increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence.” Klaudijus Januitis, head of domains at Hostinger, told me that he expects the demand for .si to keep growing, though he doesn’t see that domain replacing .ai anytime soon. Instead, as noted by that founder and his friends, Januitis said .si is right now a more available and a “more affordable second option.” “Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .ai and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury. For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment. “For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. It found that among its customers, almost 4,300 registered .si on September 30 and about 5,400 on October 1; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in the last two days. It found that more than half the buyers were coming from the U.S. and India.

Curiously enough, on Hostinger, only around 3% of the .si domains are explicitly related to AI, it said. Most are “unclassified” — meaning their names don’t match any specific category. It said that most of those registering the .si domain name seem to be people and businesses, though there is a speculative element, in that people could be buying the domains to resell them later.

Upon hearing this, my first thought went back to what a founder messaged me earlier this week, noting that .si domains were reselling for over a million dollars. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, who specializes in working with AI and crypto founders, told me that he already bought the .si version of his company name “to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai.” And did so because it was cheap, so he figured he might as well “secure it now than potentially pay a lot more later.”

Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet. “A few founder friends are buying too ’cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued. “Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.”

There is a chance that .si could become pretty popular. President Trump’s executive order said that “the capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence,” and that they “increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence.”

Instead, as noted by that founder and his friends, Januitis said .si is right now a more available and a “more affordable second option.”

“Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .ai and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury. For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment. “For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. sources.title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Blackstone’s Jas Khaira on building the next generation of AI giants
passages: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , Jas Khaira, global head of Blackstone N1, will take the Builders Stage for “Building the Next Generation of AI Giants.” He’ll share what Blackstone looks for when backing category-defining companies, how founders should think about capital as they scale, and what distinguishes lasting businesses from early traction.
For AI founders, raising capital may be one milestone.
Deciding how to use it to build a company that lasts is a much bigger challenge.
Fast growth can attract customers, employees, and investors.
One recent Blackstone investment illustrates the scale.
Blackstone and co-investors agreed to invest up to $600 million in primary equity in Indian AI infrastructure company Neysa , which planned to raise an additional $600 million in debt financing.
Capital is flowing into more than infrastructure.
In July, Anthropic launched Ode with Anthropic , an AI implementation company backed through a $1.5 billion joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, Goldman Sachs and others.

Those investments put Blackstone close to some of the biggest questions surrounding AI growth: where capital is needed, which opportunities warrant it, and what businesses have the potential to endure.

extraction.body: AI startups can grow at a speed that would have been difficult to imagine a generation ago. But rapid growth comes with another reality: scaling AI can require enormous amounts of capital, and founders have to make financing decisions long before they know whether early momentum will turn into an enduring business. sources.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX completes launch triple-header; Rocket Lab nets big contract
passages: SpaceX completes three launches in 13 hours .
SpaceX pulled off two Falcon 9 rocket launches and a Falcon Heavy mission in less than 13 hours Thursday, marking one of the busiest days ever for the company’s launch teams.
A few hours later, another Falcon 9 lifted off from California on a rideshare mission.
The launch of SpaceX’s triple-body Falcon Heavy rocket with a classified National Reconnaissance Office payload from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, rounded out the triple-header Thursday night.
Little is publicly known about the payload except that it launched into a highly inclined orbit, flying northeast from Florida’s Space Coast.
That makes three launches and four landings (plus a Dragon docking at the ISS) in one day.
Rocket Lab scores its biggest launch contract yet .
Rocket Lab has signed what it calls its largest Electron launch service agreement to date, a 20-mission agreement with Synspective, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports .
Synspective is a Japanese company with a growing fleet of radar Earth-imaging satellites.
The most recent Rocket Lab launch for Synspective occurred last Friday, September 25.
The latest agreement extends Synspective’s total bookings with Rocket Lab to 47 launches, including the 13 already flown.

“Signing 20 launches in a single deal is a massive vote of confidence not just in Electron but in the launch cadence, mission reliability, and orbital precision that Rocket Lab consistently delivers,” Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said in a statement.
This week, SpaceX celebrated the first orbital launch of its new Starship rocket.
Starship had gone 99 percent of the way to orbit before, only held back by safety concerns around the possibility of stranding the huge rocket in space.
It could carry up to 12.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit.
If all goes well, Kolias said, the company could be ready to launch by 2032.
SpaceX rideshare launch deploys 130 payloads.
The rideshare mission, known as Transporter-18, carried 130 payloads into a polar Sun-synchronous orbit.
NASA will pay to human-rate ULA’s Vulcan rocket .

NASA announced on Monday that it will exercise options to purchase two additional flights on Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, as well as financially support the company in its efforts to return the crewed vehicle to flight and find a new rocket after the Atlas V vehicle retires, Ars reports .

Bread and butter … Much of the growing ecosystem of commercial satellite startups sees SpaceX’s rideshare launches as key enablers to their businesses, offering relatively inexpensive access to space on a predictable schedule.
These kinds of launches, at least on Falcon 9, will likely go away in a couple of years as SpaceX transitions to the much larger Starship rocket.
The customers on Transporter-18 ranged from tech powerhouses like Google to scrappy startups like Starfish Space, alongside top remote sensing companies such as Planet Labs and ICEYE.
SpaceX’s Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday.
It was the 14th test flight of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle.
This time, however, the rocket’s massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity, Ars reports .
Welcome to Edition 9.13 of the Rocket Report!
The commander, Jessica Watkins, became the first Black woman to lead a mission into space.
Her crewmate, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, went to space while he and his wife are expecting their third child later this year.
R-2 V2? … Canada Rocket Company is following the lead of several US launch providers in going for a bigger rocket.

What was most notable for SpaceX with this Starship flight was that it unlocked a massive growth potential for Starlink, with the first 26 of the network’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites successfully deployed Monday.
It looks like Orbex’s Prime rocket, which never ventured near a launch pad, is still dead.

A few hours later, another Falcon 9 lifted off from California on a rideshare mission.
The launch of SpaceX’s triple-body Falcon Heavy rocket with a classified National Reconnaissance Office payload from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, rounded out the triple-header Thursday night.
Little is publicly known about the payload except that it launched into a highly inclined orbit, flying northeast from Florida’s Space Coast.
That makes three launches and four landings (plus a Dragon docking at the ISS) in one day.
Rocket Lab scores its biggest launch contract yet .
Rocket Lab has signed what it calls its largest Electron launch service agreement to date, a 20-mission agreement with Synspective, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports .
Synspective is a Japanese company with a growing fleet of radar Earth-imaging satellites.
The most recent Rocket Lab launch for Synspective occurred last Friday, September 25.
The latest agreement extends Synspective’s total bookings with Rocket Lab to 47 launches, including the 13 already flown.

“Signing 20 launches in a single deal is a massive vote of confidence not just in Electron but in the launch cadence, mission reliability, and orbital precision that Rocket Lab consistently delivers,” Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said in a statement.
This week, SpaceX celebrated the first orbital launch of its new Starship rocket.
Starship had gone 99 percent of the way to orbit before, only held back by safety concerns around the possibility of stranding the huge rocket in space.
It could carry up to 12.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit.
If all goes well, Kolias said, the company could be ready to launch by 2032.
SpaceX rideshare launch deploys 130 payloads.
The rideshare mission, known as Transporter-18, carried 130 payloads into a polar Sun-synchronous orbit.
NASA will pay to human-rate ULA’s Vulcan rocket .

NASA announced on Monday that it will exercise options to purchase two additional flights on Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, as well as financially support the company in its efforts to return the crewed vehicle to flight and find a new rocket after the Atlas V vehicle retires, Ars reports .

Bread and butter … Much of the growing ecosystem of commercial satellite startups sees SpaceX’s rideshare launches as key enablers to their businesses, offering relatively inexpensive access to space on a predictable schedule.
These kinds of launches, at least on Falcon 9, will likely go away in a couple of years as SpaceX transitions to the much larger Starship rocket.
The customers on Transporter-18 ranged from tech powerhouses like Google to scrappy startups like Starfish Space, alongside top remote sensing companies such as Planet Labs and ICEYE.
SpaceX’s Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday.
It was the 14th test flight of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle.
This time, however, the rocket’s massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity, Ars reports .
Welcome to Edition 9.13 of the Rocket Report!
The commander, Jessica Watkins, became the first Black woman to lead a mission into space.
Her crewmate, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, went to space while he and his wife are expecting their third child later this year.
R-2 V2? … Canada Rocket Company is following the lead of several US launch providers in going for a bigger rocket.

What was most notable for SpaceX with this Starship flight was that it unlocked a massive growth potential for Starlink, with the first 26 of the network’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites successfully deployed Monday.
It looks like Orbex’s Prime rocket, which never ventured near a launch pad, is still dead.

extraction.body: Blue Origin seeks FAA approval for up to 50 New Glenn launches and 50 booster landings per year. Welcome to Edition 9.13 of the Rocket Report! This week, SpaceX celebrated the first orbital launch of its new Starship rocket. I’m not sure many people, at least those outside of SpaceX, expected it to take 14 flights of Starship before it technically reached low-Earth orbit, but Monday morning’s launch finally added that to SpaceX’s list of accomplishments with its new super-heavy rocket. Starship had gone 99 percent of the way to orbit before, only held back by safety concerns around the possibility of stranding the huge rocket in space. What was most notable for SpaceX with this Starship flight was that it unlocked a massive growth potential for Starlink, with the first 26 of the network’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites successfully deployed Monday. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Rocket Lab scores its biggest launch contract yet . Rocket Lab has signed what it calls its largest Electron launch service agreement to date, a 20-mission agreement with Synspective, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports . Synspective is a Japanese company with a growing fleet of radar Earth-imaging satellites. It is one of Rocket Lab’s most loyal customers, with the company’s light-class Electron rocket having launched 13 of Synspective’s StriX radar sats since 2020. The most recent Rocket Lab launch for Synspective occurred last Friday, September 25. Dedicated launch … Rocket Lab’s Electron launch vehicle is sized for dedicated launches of payloads like Synspective’s StriX satellites. The latest agreement extends Synspective’s total bookings with Rocket Lab to 47 launches, including the 13 already flown. “Signing 20 launches in a single deal is a massive vote of confidence not just in Electron but in the launch cadence, mission reliability, and orbital precision that Rocket Lab consistently delivers,” Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said in a statement. Portuguese company acquires what’s left of Orbex . A Portuguese space technology business has snapped up the assets of Orbex, the Scottish rocket maker that collapsed earlier this year, the Scotsman reports . The buyer, Omnidea, plans to establish its UK operations at Orbex’s former manufacturing facility in Scotland, having agreed to a deal to acquire the assets and intellectual property (IP) of the defunct rocket developer. An initial team of ex-Orbex employees will join the business, with Omnidea planning to recruit further as the operation develops. No Prime resurrection … Omnidea, once a partner of Orbex, says it plans to use its new Scotland base as a center for “structures development and fabrication” and as a “hub for flight and ground system electronics.” Omnidea is a supplier of propulsion, fluid control, avionics, and thermal management components in the European space industry, but the company is also exploring other markets. It looks like Orbex’s Prime rocket, which never ventured near a launch pad, is still dead. Crew-13 launches toward ISS . A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station, Ars reports . Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening. Some notes … This mission is nothing particularly new for SpaceX (it’s the company’s 21st human spaceflight launch). But it is noteworthy for a few reasons. The commander, Jessica Watkins, became the first Black woman to lead a mission into space. Her crewmate, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, went to space while he and his wife are expecting their third child later this year. It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter in Houston. This launch was delayed several weeks to fix a leaky valve on Dragon’s propulsion system, work that involved cutting out the suspect valve and welding in a new one, an unusual but apparently successful repair method. Canadian company pursues medium-lift rocket . More countries are becoming interested in developing their own access to space, including those that have historically paid US companies to launch their satellites. Canada is no different, and the Trump administration’s seeming obsession with lobbing threats and tariffs across the northern border has only crystallized Canadian interest in sovereign access to space. This spring, the Canadian government announced the first awards to three companies—NordSpace, Reaction Dynamics, and Canada Rocket Company—to support work on rockets with “light lift” capability. Now, one of these rocket developers, Canada Rocket Company, says it is skipping over the small launch segment and going straight to a more ambitious medium-lift rocket, Ars reports . R-2 V2? … Canada Rocket Company is following the lead of several US launch providers in going for a bigger rocket. “The advice we got from having spoken with about 150 engineers, from the director of Starship engineering all the way down to some entry-level folks, is that you’re not going to be able to de-risk a rocket development program by building a smaller rocket,” said Hugh Kolias, chief executive of the Canada Rocket Company, in an interview with Ars. The company’s R-2 rocket somewhat resembles SpaceX’s Falcon 9 in renderings, with nine engines and landing legs that signal a future path toward reuse of the first stage. It could carry up to 12.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit. If all goes well, Kolias said, the company could be ready to launch by 2032. SpaceX rideshare launch deploys 130 payloads. An artificial intelligence prototype from Google, a methane-tracker, pharmaceutical manufacturing labs, and more hitched a ride onboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on Thursday afternoon, Spaceflight Now reports . The rideshare mission, known as Transporter-18, carried 130 payloads into a polar Sun-synchronous orbit. It was SpaceX’s second launch of the day, following the successful flight of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission from Florida a few hours earlier. Bread and butter … Much of the growing ecosystem of commercial satellite startups sees SpaceX’s rideshare launches as key enablers to their businesses, offering relatively inexpensive access to space on a predictable schedule. These kinds of launches, at least on Falcon 9, will likely go away in a couple of years as SpaceX transitions to the much larger Starship rocket. But for now, a bevy of satellite companies continue relying on Falcon 9 launches. The customers on Transporter-18 ranged from tech powerhouses like Google to scrappy startups like Starfish Space, alongside top remote sensing companies such as Planet Labs and ICEYE. Starship reaches new heights in low-Earth orbit. SpaceX’s Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday. It was the 14th test flight of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle. This time, however, the rocket’s massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity, Ars reports . On all of Starship’s previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth’s gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did. Debuting Starlink V3 … What’s more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company’s newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket’s cargo bay. One by one, the flat-packed satellites —too large to fit inside SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket —were released from Starship’s payload deployer using a system of pulleys and cables to eject the satellites overboard like a Pez dispenser spits out candy. SpaceX cut a planned 10-hour test flight to three hours after one of the ship’s Raptor engines failed during ascent, but the vehicle was still able to make a pinpoint splashdown at one of its backup return sites north of Hawaii. NASA will pay to human-rate ULA’s Vulcan rocket . NASA announced on Monday that it will exercise options to purchase two additional flights on Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, as well as financially support the company in its efforts to return the crewed vehicle to flight and find a new rocket after the Atlas V vehicle retires, Ars reports . NASA is making the moves to preserve a path for its astronauts to low-Earth orbit as SpaceX nears retirement of its Falcon 9 rocket and Crew Dragon spacecraft. When that happens, Boeing’s troubled Starliner spacecraft will likely be the only commercial means of launching US crews to orbit. A post-Atlas future … During a news conference on Monday, Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, said the space agency would pay $359 million to Boeing to help the company complete a rebuild of the reaction control system thrusters that have overheated in flight. It would also certify United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket for human missions. NASA also said it would exercise options to order two additional crewed missions on Starliner, bringing its total spaceflights on the vehicle to six. Any future Starliner flights beyond that would require a new rocket, like ULA’s Vulcan, as the Atlas V rocket is no longer in production. SpaceX completes three launches in 13 hours . SpaceX pulled off two Falcon 9 rocket launches and a Falcon Heavy mission in less than 13 hours Thursday, marking one of the busiest days ever for the company’s launch teams. The action began, as noted previously in the Rocket Report, with a Falcon 9 launch from Cape Canaveral, Florida, carrying the next four-person crew to the International Space Station. A few hours later, another Falcon 9 lifted off from California on a rideshare mission. The launch of SpaceX’s triple-body Falcon Heavy rocket with a classified National Reconnaissance Office payload from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, rounded out the triple-header Thursday night. And four landings … This was the first time a Falcon Heavy rocket has launched a payload for the NRO, the US government’s spy satellite agency. Little is publicly known about the payload except that it launched into a highly inclined orbit, flying northeast from Florida’s Space Coast. To add an extra flourish to the launch triple-header, SpaceX returned both Falcon 9 boosters to their launch sites in Florida and California and landed both side boosters from Falcon Heavy back at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. That makes three launches and four landings (plus a Dragon docking at the ISS) in one day. Blue Origin foresees growing launch cadence . As Blue Origin continues to recover from a New Glenn pad explosion in May, the company is seeking permission to significantly increase the vehicle’s launch rate, Space News reports . This is a big surprise, but a draft environmental assessment released this week puts some numbers to Blue Origin’s plans. The company is seeking permission from the FAA to increase the rate of New Glenn launches from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station’s Launch Complex 36 from 12 to 50 per year. Reuse built in … The proposal would include 50 launches of the rocket and 50 landings of the rocket’s first stage on a drone ship in the Atlantic Ocean. It would also allow up to 100 static-fire tests, one for each stage of the rocket for each launch. The proposal also covers recovery of the rocket’s payload fairing, which Blue Origin has not attempted on any of the three launches of New Glenn to date. October 5 : Falcon 9 | SDA Tranche 1 Transport Layer A | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 08:17 UTC

A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station, Ars reports . Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening.

Some notes … This mission is nothing particularly new for SpaceX (it’s the company’s 21st human spaceflight launch). But it is noteworthy for a few reasons. The commander, Jessica Watkins, became the first Black woman to lead a mission into space. Her crewmate, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, went to space while he and his wife are expecting their third child later this year.

It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter in Houston. This launch was delayed several weeks to fix a leaky valve on Dragon’s propulsion system, work that involved cutting out the suspect valve and welding in a new one, an unusual but apparently successful repair method.

Canadian company pursues medium-lift rocket . More countries are becoming interested in developing their own access to space, including those that have historically paid US companies to launch their satellites. Canada is no different, and the Trump administration’s seeming obsession with lobbing threats and tariffs across the northern border has only crystallized Canadian interest in sovereign access to space.

This spring, the Canadian government announced the first awards to three companies—NordSpace, Reaction Dynamics, and Canada Rocket Company—to support work on rockets with “light lift” capability. Now, one of these rocket developers, Canada Rocket Company, says it is skipping over the small launch segment and going straight to a more ambitious medium-lift rocket, Ars reports .

R-2 V2? … Canada Rocket Company is following the lead of several US launch providers in going for a bigger rocket. “The advice we got from having spoken with about 150 engineers, from the director of Starship engineering all the way down to some entry-level folks, is that you’re not going to be able to de-risk a rocket development program by building a smaller rocket,” said Hugh Kolias, chief executive of the Canada Rocket Company, in an interview with Ars.

The company’s R-2 rocket somewhat resembles SpaceX’s Falcon 9 in renderings, with nine engines and landing legs that signal a future path toward reuse of the first stage. It could carry up to 12.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit. If all goes well, Kolias said, the company could be ready to launch by 2032.

SpaceX rideshare launch deploys 130 payloads. An artificial intelligence prototype from Google, a methane-tracker, pharmaceutical manufacturing labs, and more hitched a ride onboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on Thursday afternoon, Spaceflight Now reports . The rideshare mission, known as Transporter-18, carried 130 payloads into a polar Sun-synchronous orbit. It was SpaceX’s second launch of the day, following the successful flight of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission from Florida a few hours earlier.

Bread and butter … Much of the growing ecosystem of commercial satellite startups sees SpaceX’s rideshare launches as key enablers to their businesses, offering relatively inexpensive access to space on a predictable schedule. These kinds of launches, at least on Falcon 9, will likely go away in a couple of years as SpaceX transitions to the much larger Starship rocket. But for now, a bevy of satellite companies continue relying on Falcon 9 launches. The customers on Transporter-18 ranged from tech powerhouses like Google to scrappy startups like Starfish Space, alongside top remote sensing companies such as Planet Labs and ICEYE.

Starship reaches new heights in low-Earth orbit. SpaceX’s Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday. It was the 14th test flight of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle. This time, however, the rocket’s massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity, Ars reports .

On all of Starship’s previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth’s gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did.

Debuting Starlink V3 … What’s more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company’s newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket’s cargo bay. One by one, the flat-packed satellites —too large to fit inside SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket —were released from Starship’s payload deployer using a system of pulleys and cables to eject the satellites overboard like a Pez dispenser spits out candy. SpaceX cut a planned 10-hour test flight to three hours after one of the ship’s Raptor engines failed during ascent, but the vehicle was still able to make a pinpoint splashdown at one of its backup return sites north of Hawaii.

NASA will pay to human-rate ULA’s Vulcan rocket . NASA announced on Monday that it will exercise options to purchase two additional flights on Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, as well as financially support the company in its efforts to return the crewed vehicle to flight and find a new rocket after the Atlas V vehicle retires, Ars reports . NASA is making the moves to preserve a path for its astronauts to low-Earth orbit as SpaceX nears retirement of its Falcon 9 rocket and Crew Dragon spacecraft. When that happens, Boeing’s troubled Starliner spacecraft will likely be the only commercial means of launching US crews to orbit.

A post-Atlas future … During a news conference on Monday, Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, said the space agency would pay $359 million to Boeing to help the company complete a rebuild of the reaction control system thrusters that have overheated in flight. It would also certify United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket for human missions. NASA also said it would exercise options to order two additional crewed missions on Starliner, bringing its total spaceflights on the vehicle to six. Any future Starliner flights beyond that would require a new rocket, like ULA’s Vulcan, as the Atlas V rocket is no longer in production.

SpaceX completes three launches in 13 hours . SpaceX pulled off two Falcon 9 rocket launches and a Falcon Heavy mission in less than 13 hours Thursday, marking one of the busiest days ever for the company’s launch teams. The action began, as noted previously in the Rocket Report, with a Falcon 9 launch from Cape Canaveral, Florida, carrying the next four-person crew to the International Space Station. A few hours later, another Falcon 9 lifted off from California on a rideshare mission. The launch of SpaceX’s triple-body Falcon Heavy rocket with a classified National Reconnaissance Office payload from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, rounded out the triple-header Thursday night.

And four landings … This was the first time a Falcon Heavy rocket has launched a payload for the NRO, the US government’s spy satellite agency. Little is publicly known about the payload except that it launched into a highly inclined orbit, flying northeast from Florida’s Space Coast. To add an extra flourish to the launch triple-header, SpaceX returned both Falcon 9 boosters to their launch sites in Florida and California and landed both side boosters from Falcon Heavy back at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. That makes three launches and four landings (plus a Dragon docking at the ISS) in one day.

Blue Origin foresees growing launch cadence . As Blue Origin continues to recover from a New Glenn pad explosion in May, the company is seeking permission to significantly increase the vehicle’s launch rate, Space News reports . This is a big surprise, but a draft environmental assessment released this week puts some numbers to Blue Origin’s plans. The company is seeking permission from the FAA to increase the rate of New Glenn launches from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station’s Launch Complex 36 from 12 to 50 per year.

Reuse built in … The proposal would include 50 launches of the rocket and 50 landings of the rocket’s first stage on a drone ship in the Atlantic Ocean. It would also allow up to 100 static-fire tests, one for each stage of the rocket for each launch. The proposal also covers recovery of the rocket’s payload fairing, which Blue Origin has not attempted on any of the three launches of New Glenn to date.

passages: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era?
Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that, based on the feedback we’ve gotten from the community and the reality on the ground.
If you’re asking Claude or ChatGPT if TechCrunch Disrupt is worth it, you’re not alone.
The reality is that Disrupt is a unique event, and it’s happening at a unique time for the startup community.
This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it.
Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology.
That’s not the exception at Disrupt — that’s the point.
And those opportunities aren’t just available for Battlefield finalists.
Every conversation in the Expo Hall or in a Side Event can create an opportunity for your startup.
For years, whether it’s been held in New York, San Francisco, or elsewhere, Disrupt has brought together thousands of founders, investors, startup team members, and tech leaders.
Check out the full lineup of speakers across all stages and events here .
Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app.
You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors.
Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed — there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find.
The 200 startups chosen on August 20 to compete go through a rigorous prep process and get the opportunity to pitch onstage in front of top-tier VCs and the Disrupt crowds.
You’ll also get to watch those pitches, take notes, learn from the peaks and valleys, and potentially meet the teams behind the ideas and innovations.
It could be in a follow-up meeting or just walking through the halls of Moscone.
Last year at Disrupt, we spoke with founders about their experiences and discovered the results of their attendance firsthand.
And if that all leaves you inspired, here’s an insider tip: Most Battlefield participants, and several winners, have gone through the process multiple times.

If there are colleagues in your network who have been impacted by layoffs who you’d like to have join up, we have an option for them as well, with a special $75 Expo+ Pass available at a limited volume for those impacted by cutbacks this year .
But it’s the lead-up to that $100,000 check and the deluge of attention the winner receives that’s the most valuable for founders attending Disrupt.

Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology. Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app. You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors. And when your schedule isn’t packed with dealmaking, learn from VC perspectives and fundraising-focused sessions at the Builders Stage . You’re here in search of talent, strategic partners, and market visibility. Those same networking tools and opportunities can help you meet potential hires and partners and deepen those connections or make new ones. Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed — there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find. extraction.body: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era? Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that, based on the feedback we’ve gotten from the community and the reality on the ground. Last year at Disrupt, we spoke with founders about their experiences and discovered the results of their attendance firsthand. One founder saw a 3x oversubscription rate after their confirmation for Startup Battlefield and more than 100 investor inbounds helping fuel conversations about a future fundraising round. Another founder had nearly 30 back-to-back conversations with investors who flocked to them after a pitch onstage and followed them to their booth . That’s not the exception at Disrupt — that’s the point. And those opportunities aren’t just available for Battlefield finalists. Every conversation in the Expo Hall or in a Side Event can create an opportunity for your startup. For years, whether it’s been held in New York, San Francisco, or elsewhere, Disrupt has brought together thousands of founders, investors, startup team members, and tech leaders. We’re keeping that mission alive at SF’s Moscone West, this October 13-15 with a packed lineup of speakers, more than 200 expert sessions, a wealth of organized and serendipitous networking opportunities, and most of all, the chance to be in the same room as the person who could change your nascent idea for a company or your current startup’s trajectory. If you’re asking Claude or ChatGPT if TechCrunch Disrupt is worth it, you’re not alone. The reality is that Disrupt is a unique event, and it’s happening at a unique time for the startup community. This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it. Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology. Whether you’re raising your first round, scaling your team, or deciding how AI changes your product, every session is designed to answer one question: “What can I take back to my company on Monday morning?” Disrupt works a bit differently, depending on where you are in your founding journey, with different tracks you can follow to make the most of the three days: You’re here for capital and validation above all else, and your time is valuable. Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app. You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors. And when your schedule isn’t packed with dealmaking, learn from VC perspectives and fundraising-focused sessions at the Builders Stage . You’re here in search of talent, strategic partners, and market visibility. Those same networking tools and opportunities can help you meet potential hires and partners and deepen those connections or make new ones. Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed — there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find. The Startup Battlefield winner’s reveal packs the Disrupt stage and is each year’s capstone event. But it’s the lead-up to that $100,000 check and the deluge of attention the winner receives that’s the most valuable for founders attending Disrupt. The 200 startups chosen on August 20 to compete go through a rigorous prep process and get the opportunity to pitch onstage in front of top-tier VCs and the Disrupt crowds. You’ll also get to watch those pitches, take notes, learn from the peaks and valleys, and potentially meet the teams behind the ideas and innovations. It could be in a follow-up meeting or just walking through the halls of Moscone. And if that all leaves you inspired, here’s an insider tip: Most Battlefield participants, and several winners, have gone through the process multiple times. We’re no longer taking applications for 2026’s competition, but we’re expanding the program to more international markets, and the 2027 process will be similar to this year’s , so take note for the future! Disrupt 2026 spans several stages , each built around a different founder need: And that’s just the beginning — we’ll have more speakers to announce as we get closer to Disrupt. Check out the full lineup of speakers across all stages and events here . If there are colleagues in your network who have been impacted by layoffs who you’d like to have join up, we have an option for them as well, with a special $75 Expo+ Pass available at a limited volume for those impacted by cutbacks this year . Your time at Disrupt is valuable, too, so before you head there, check on our regularly updated schedule of speakers and Side Events , get ahead of competitors’ schedules by booking your networking opportunities in advance, and get your own elevator pitches in order to make the most of those magical Disrupt moments that can come at any point October 13-15! extraction.body: Composable infrastructure, sovereign data, and cross-functional coordination can enable intelligence to flow and AI to grow smarter. Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition. It is in full operational flight. Model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can absorb, while the cost of performance continues to fall. Globally, AI investment is set to reach $2.5 trillion in 2026, up 44% from the previous year. For many enterprises, this investment has produced fragmentation. Intelligence can accumulate in silos so that sales agents are unaware of open support tickets, for instance, or marketing systems are personalizing content without visibility into what finance already knows about a customer. Each function may perform well in isolation, but the enterprise as a whole learns little and has less information to act upon. The shift from AI as a tool to AI as an operating model—what we call the “agentic shift” in this report—demands something more fundamental than better models or faster infrastructure. It requires connecting people, processes, and data in real time, along with the governance and control to act on that intelligence reliably. This means rethinking both architecture and operating models simultaneously. First, rebuilding data infrastructure for accessibility rather than volume. Second, replacing fixed tech stacks with composable architectures that can evolve as models and tools change. And, lastly, resolving questions of AI sovereignty, including where intelligence runs, who controls it, and how it operates across organizational and jurisdictional boundaries. Enterprise AI’s scaling problem is structural. Process-first companies are pulling ahead. Global AI spending is rising sharply and model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can integrate them. Yet the majority of enterprises are still not growing revenue through AI or fundamentally rethinking how they operate. The companies generating sustained returns share a common discipline. They treat process redesign as the work that precedes model selection, building for how the technology will evolve rather than retrofitting roles and workflows after deployment. For them, the agentic shift begins with the operating model. Data readiness, not data abundance, is what makes AI compoundable. Most enterprises discover too late that having data and having AI-ready data are very different things. A sovereign, composable foundation—one that queries and prepares data where it resides, without migration or centralization—can convert raw data estates into intelligence that AI agents can act upon. As data residency laws, multicloud environments, and structural complexity make centralization increasingly impractical, sovereign control over where models run and data lives is what keeps that adaptability intact. sources.title: Medical records giant Epic pauses product development to fix security bugs that risk patients' data - TechCrunch
passages: Epic, the software technology giant that makes the widely used MyChart software for accessing patients’ medical data, has paused most of its product development as the company works to protect its software and systems from cyberattacks.

Judy Faulkner, the founder and chief executive of Epic, told Modern Healthcare last month that the pause would likely last six weeks while work continues on “safeguarding” the company’s products, after a deployment of Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity model Mythos unearthed security flaws that could allow access to patients’ data.
But a bug unknown to Epic could allow hackers to compromise multiple MyChart affected systems located across the United States and raid the data stored within.

Martin, who did not return TechCrunch’s request for comment, told the Times that the AI model did not say if the bug could be exploited to alter patient records without detection, but argued it was enough of a risk to remediate the issues.

It’s rare for a company to pause development to fix security bugs, but the advent of AI tools capable of rapidly finding and exploiting security vulnerabilities has led to concerns that attackers could have an easier time at stealing data.

This includes medical records stolen during a breach at electronic health data storage giant CareCloud , millions of rows of patient data from pharmaceutical distributor McKesson , and an unspecified amount of stolen data from U.K.-based health tech company Craneware, whose software is used across North America.
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.

Judy Faulkner, the founder and chief executive of Epic, told Modern Healthcare last month that the pause would likely last six weeks while work continues on “safeguarding” the company’s products, after a deployment of Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity model Mythos unearthed security flaws that could allow access to patients’ data. The company has not disclosed the nature of the bugs, but its chief security officer Stirling Martin told The New York Times that some customer configurations of MyChart could allow outsiders to access patient records without recording any intrusion in the software’s logs. Martin, who did not return TechCrunch’s request for comment, told the Times that the AI model did not say if the bug could be exploited to alter patient records without detection, but argued it was enough of a risk to remediate the issues. Epic’s widely used MyChart software is used to maintain over 320 million patient records across hospitals and doctor’s offices across the United States. Epic says it does not have access to customers’ medical data: that responsibility falls on healthcare providers like hospitals and doctor’s offices. But a bug unknown to Epic could allow hackers to compromise multiple MyChart affected systems located across the United States and raid the data stored within. Healthcare breaches are increasingly common as hackers seek access to highly sensitive health and medical data, under the assumption that providers would pay to prevent hackers from publishing the information online. A 2024 ransomware attack on Change Healthcare , a health tech company owned by insurance giant UnitedHealth tasked with handling payments and billing for most Americans, allowed hackers to steal health data on more than 192 million people, the majority of people in the United States. The company paid the hackers twice not to publish the stolen data. This year, a string of back-to-back data breaches at healthcare and tech companies have affected tens of millions of Americans. This includes medical records stolen during a breach at electronic health data storage giant CareCloud , millions of rows of patient data from pharmaceutical distributor McKesson , and an unspecified amount of stolen data from U.K.-based health tech company Craneware, whose software is used across North America. The Department of Health and Human Services currently lists a breach at dental insurance company DentaQuest affecting 15 million people as the largest healthcare-related data breach of 2026 so far. Judy Faulkner, the founder and chief executive of Epic, told Modern Healthcare last month that the pause would likely last six weeks while work continues on “safeguarding” the company’s products, after a deployment of Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity model Mythos unearthed security flaws that could allow access to patients’ data.

The company has not disclosed the nature of the bugs, but its chief security officer Stirling Martin told The New York Times that some customer configurations of MyChart could allow outsiders to access patient records without recording any intrusion in the software’s logs.

Martin, who did not return TechCrunch’s request for comment, told the Times that the AI model did not say if the bug could be exploited to alter patient records without detection, but argued it was enough of a risk to remediate the issues.

Epic’s widely used MyChart software is used to maintain over 320 million patient records across hospitals and doctor’s offices across the United States. Epic says it does not have access to customers’ medical data: that responsibility falls on healthcare providers like hospitals and doctor’s offices. But a bug unknown to Epic could allow hackers to compromise multiple MyChart affected systems located across the United States and raid the data stored within.

It’s rare for a company to pause development to fix security bugs, but the advent of AI tools capable of rapidly finding and exploiting security vulnerabilities has led to concerns that attackers could have an easier time at stealing data.

Healthcare breaches are increasingly common as hackers seek access to highly sensitive health and medical data, under the assumption that providers would pay to prevent hackers from publishing the information online. A 2024 ransomware attack on Change Healthcare , a health tech company owned by insurance giant UnitedHealth tasked with handling payments and billing for most Americans, allowed hackers to steal health data on more than 192 million people, the majority of people in the United States. The company paid the hackers twice not to publish the stolen data.

This year, a string of back-to-back data breaches at healthcare and tech companies have affected tens of millions of Americans. This includes medical records stolen during a breach at electronic health data storage giant CareCloud , millions of rows of patient data from pharmaceutical distributor McKesson , and an unspecified amount of stolen data from U.K.-based health tech company Craneware, whose software is used across North America.
The Department of Health and Human Services currently lists a breach at dental insurance company DentaQuest affecting 15 million people as the largest healthcare-related data breach of 2026 so far.

passages: Kevin Mandia, best known as the founder of cybersecurity startup Mandiant, which sold to Google for $5.4 billion in 2022 , has raised $255.5 million for his latest startup, Armadin, at a valuation of more than $2.5 billion, the company announced on Thursday.
Armadin is offering enterprises a new kind of always-on security by reimagining defense testing for the AI era.

Instead of traditional penetration tests, where hired guns attempt to break in and report on the weaknesses they find, Armadin runs always-on agentic swarms, who chain together vulnerabilities to hack in.
The idea is to help organizations find and seal holes before any bad guys (or even AI labs with rogue agents ) can use agentic tech against them.
The new round comes just six months after Armadin raised a $190 million Series A in March.

passages: A California business owner was arrested on Thursday after being charged with allegedly smuggling Nvidia hardware to China without the proper export licenses.
Keeping the highest-end GPUs out of Chinese hands has been a priority for the US government.

Greg Lui, 38, allegedly tried to export around $300 million worth of Nvidia kit - typically used for artificial intelligence (AI) development - via US-based freight businesses and Malaysian transshipment companies.
The Register contacted Earthmade and Nvidia for comment. ®

Prosecutors allege that Lui used his company, Earthmade Computer Inc, to order the products in the US, which consisted of servers containing high-powered Nvidia components, including A100, H100, PNY GE Force RTX 4090, and GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs.

Lui would then send them to Malaysia and Singapore, two countries that do not require licenses from the Commerce Department, and companies there would forward them to China in an effort to circumvent US export controls .
His alleged crimes violate regulations prohibiting the sale of economically sensitive equipment to adversarial countries, such as China, in the interests of national security.
Prosecutors claim Greg Lui helped China procure advanced hardware to develop, ahem, 'super intelligence’

A California business owner was arrested on Thursday after being charged with allegedly smuggling Nvidia hardware to China without the proper export licenses. Keeping the highest-end GPUs out of Chinese hands has been a priority for the US government.

Greg Lui, 38, allegedly tried to export around $300 million worth of Nvidia kit - typically used for artificial intelligence (AI) development - via US-based freight businesses and Malaysian transshipment companies.

Prosecutors allege that Lui used his company, Earthmade Computer Inc, to order the products in the US, which consisted of servers containing high-powered Nvidia components, including A100, H100, PNY GE Force RTX 4090, and GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs.

Lui would then send them to Malaysia and Singapore, two countries that do not require licenses from the Commerce Department, and companies there would forward them to China in an effort to circumvent US export controls .
His alleged crimes violate regulations prohibiting the sale of economically sensitive equipment to adversarial countries, such as China, in the interests of national security.
In lay terms, the US doesn’t want its own tech companies’ high-end hardware being used to accelerate China’s push for dominance in the race for the world’s most capable AI.
Or, as it’s referred to in the US nowadays, “ super intelligence (SI).”

“SI is the defining technology of the era,” said John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security. “The National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology, a product of our unparalleled innovation and hard work, from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries.”
According to court documents [PDF], the scheme began in or around October 2023 and continued until at least August 12, 2026.

Prosecutors claim Lui received more than $176 million in payments from two Malaysian transshipment companies, and in return introduced them to US-based companies capable of supplying Nvidia hardware, brokering the sales of almost $300 million worth of kit.

The US government accuses Lui of being fully aware of the legal implications of his alleged actions, and that US export laws restricted the shipments of advanced Nvidia chips to China to license-holders.

Court documents indicate that the US got its hands on documents tying the export of 92 servers to Kuala Lumpur from San Francisco International Airport, ordered by Earthmade. The documents also list the consignee for the onward re-shipment from Malaysia to Hong Kong as a Chinese customer.

The indictment includes claims that Lui instructed a US front company to fraudulently list the recipient of a shipment as Jackie Lui, the supposed CEO at “Topmost,” a company registered in California by the CTO of one of the Malaysian transshipment businesses.
Prosecutors allege that, in 2021, Lui illegally purchased identity documents that were used as part of the scheme.

Lui is charged with one count each of violations related to the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, outbound smuggling, and money laundering, which together carry a maximum prison sentence of 50 years.

“The FBI’s investigation revealed that Lui allegedly sold the Chinese government hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of American Super Intelligence technology, in clear violation of US export control laws,” said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.

“Controlling the export of advanced SI technology is critical to safeguarding our national security and defending the homeland, and the FBI will keep fighting for America’s businesses and economic security. We’re grateful to our partners across the US government and private sector for their assistance, and we’ll continue holding accountable anyone who violates US export laws to enrich themselves and help our adversaries.”
The Register contacted Earthmade and Nvidia for comment. ®

A California business owner was arrested on Thursday after being charged with allegedly smuggling Nvidia hardware to China without the proper export licenses. Keeping the highest-end GPUs out of Chinese hands has been a priority for the US government.

Greg Lui, 38, allegedly tried to export around $300 million worth of Nvidia kit - typically used for artificial intelligence (AI) development - via US-based freight businesses and Malaysian transshipment companies.

Prosecutors allege that Lui used his company, Earthmade Computer Inc, to order the products in the US, which consisted of servers containing high-powered Nvidia components, including A100, H100, PNY GE Force RTX 4090, and GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs.

Lui would then send them to Malaysia and Singapore, two countries that do not require licenses from the Commerce Department, and companies there would forward them to China in an effort to circumvent US export controls .
His alleged crimes violate regulations prohibiting the sale of economically sensitive equipment to adversarial countries, such as China, in the interests of national security.
In lay terms, the US doesn’t want its own tech companies’ high-end hardware being used to accelerate China’s push for dominance in the race for the world’s most capable AI.
Or, as it’s referred to in the US nowadays, “ super intelligence (SI).”

“SI is the defining technology of the era,” said John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security. “The National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology, a product of our unparalleled innovation and hard work, from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries.”
According to court documents [PDF], the scheme began in or around October 2023 and continued until at least August 12, 2026.

Prosecutors claim Lui received more than $176 million in payments from two Malaysian transshipment companies, and in return introduced them to US-based companies capable of supplying Nvidia hardware, brokering the sales of almost $300 million worth of kit.

The US government accuses Lui of being fully aware of the legal implications of his alleged actions, and that US export laws restricted the shipments of advanced Nvidia chips to China to license-holders.

Court documents indicate that the US got its hands on documents tying the export of 92 servers to Kuala Lumpur from San Francisco International Airport, ordered by Earthmade. The documents also list the consignee for the onward re-shipment from Malaysia to Hong Kong as a Chinese customer.

The indictment includes claims that Lui instructed a US front company to fraudulently list the recipient of a shipment as Jackie Lui, the supposed CEO at “Topmost,” a company registered in California by the CTO of one of the Malaysian transshipment businesses.
Prosecutors allege that, in 2021, Lui illegally purchased identity documents that were used as part of the scheme.

Lui is charged with one count each of violations related to the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, outbound smuggling, and money laundering, which together carry a maximum prison sentence of 50 years.

“The FBI’s investigation revealed that Lui allegedly sold the Chinese government hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of American Super Intelligence technology, in clear violation of US export control laws,” said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.

“Controlling the export of advanced SI technology is critical to safeguarding our national security and defending the homeland, and the FBI will keep fighting for America’s businesses and economic security. We’re grateful to our partners across the US government and private sector for their assistance, and we’ll continue holding accountable anyone who violates US export laws to enrich themselves and help our adversaries.”
The Register contacted Earthmade and Nvidia for comment. ®
